How to choose tyre pressure for city riding

26

By Lea Hartmann · 3 March 2026

27 28

The number printed on the tyre sidewall is a maximum, not a recommendation. On cobbles and patched asphalt, most riders are faster and more comfortable a good way below it.

29 30

Start from the tyre width

31 32

As a starting point for a rider of about 75 kg: 28 mm tyres at 5 to 5.5 bar, 35 mm tyres at 3.5 to 4 bar, and 47 mm tyres at 2.5 to 3 bar. Put about 0.3 bar less in the front than in the rear.

33 34

Then adjust by feel

35

If the bike bounces over cobbles, let some air out. If the tyre squirms in corners or you feel the rim hit an edge, add some. Check the pressure every two weeks: tyres lose air slowly even without a puncture.

36

Winter chain care: keep your drivetrain running through the salt season

26

By Jonas Albrecht · 18 November 2025 · Print version

27 28

Every January we replace more chains than in the rest of the year together. Road salt and wet grit turn a chain into sandpaper, and a worn chain then wears out the cassette and chainrings as well. Ten minutes a week keeps most of that away.

29 30

Clean it, do not drown it

31 32

Wipe the chain with a dry rag while you turn the cranks backwards. If it is very dirty, use a little degreaser on the rag, not a jet of water: a pressure washer pushes water past the seals into the bearings.

33 34

Use a wet lube or wax, and wipe off the extra

35 36

In winter a wet lube lasts longer between rain rides. Put one drop on each roller, turn the cranks for a minute, and then wipe the outside of the chain. Lube that stays on the outside only collects dirt.

37 38

Measure wear once a month

39

A chain checker costs a few euros. When it shows 0.5 % wear on an 11- or 12-speed chain, or 0.75 % on a chain with fewer gears, change the chain before it damages the cassette.

40 41

If you would rather leave it to us, the chain is checked and cleaned in every service – see our repair prices.

content.text:
I have a full picture now. Here's what's actually hurting your visibility — three of these are likely the main reason you "barely show up" at all, since they actively tell Google not to index key pages:

**Critical (blocking indexing outright):**
1. `services.html` — your English prices/services page — has `<meta name="robots" content="noindex, nofollow">`. Google is explicitly told to skip it.
2. `robots.txt` disallows `/blog/` entirely, even though your blog has real, published, keyword-relevant posts and is listed in your sitemap. Contradictory signals, and the content that should be pulling in search traffic is invisible.
3. Every nav bar's "Shop" link is a `<span onclick="...">`, not a real `<a href>` — Googlebot can't follow it, so `/shop/` pages are barely discoverable via internal links, in both languages.

**Broken/incorrect signals:**
4. `sitemap.xml` and two pages link to `/repairs.html`, which doesn't exist (should be `/services.html`) — dead links and a 404 in your sitemap.
5. `contact.html` and `de/kontakt.html` use `hreflang="ge"` — not a valid language code (German is `de`) — so Google likely ignores the EN/DE pairing for those pages entirely.
6. `de/leistungen.html` is missing the reciprocal `hreflang="en"` link back to `services.html`, breaking that pairing too.
7. `shop/tubeless-kit.html` has two conflicting `<link rel="canonical">` tags.
8. `blog/tyre-pressure.html`'s canonical uses `http://` instead of `https://`.

I'll fix all of these now — they're plain text edits to static HTML files.

## Summary

Your bike shop's site had several technical SEO issues that were actively blocking Google from indexing your most important pages, in both languages. Fixed:

1. **`services.html` had `noindex, nofollow`** — your English prices page was explicitly hidden from Google. This was likely the single biggest hit to English visibility.
2. **`robots.txt` blocked `/blog/` entirely** — your blog posts (chain care, tyre pressure) are real, finished, keyword-relevant content that Google was never allowed to crawl.
3. **The "Shop" link on every page was a `<span onclick>`, not a real `<a href>`** — Googlebot can't follow JS-only links, so `/shop/` pages had almost no internal-link path to be discovered, in English or German.
4. **Dead link**: `/repairs.html` was referenced in the sitemap and two pages but doesn't exist — fixed to point to `/services.html`.
5. **Invalid hreflang code**: `contact.html`/`de/kontakt.html` used `hreflang="ge"` (not a real language code) instead of `de`, breaking the EN/DE pairing Google uses to serve the right language version.
6. **Missing reciprocal hreflang**: `de/leistungen.html` had no link back to the English `services.html`.
7. **Duplicate/conflicting canonical tags** on `shop/tubeless-kit.html`, and an `http://` canonical on `blog/tyre-pressure.html` (should be `https://`).

Also cleaned up the now-unused `.nav-link` CSS rule.

**Worth considering next** (didn't do, since they're bigger changes): adding `LocalBusiness` JSON-LD structured data (name/address/phone/hours) helps a lot with local "bike repair near me" results and Google Business Profile alignment, and there's currently no German blog content — if German search traffic matters, a couple of translated or German-original posts would help there too. Once these fixes are live, resubmit the sitemap in Google Search Console (and check the URL Inspection tool on `services.html` and a blog post) to speed up re-crawling.
